_about: Well-known conflicts between aquarium species, kept short and cautious (#20). Names are scientific: a genus alone matches every species in it. `a` and `b` are the two sides; `text` says why, with {a} and {b} replaced by the common names kept in the tank. Rules with `min` warn when that many or more of one species share a tank.

pairs.text: Bettas and guppies often don't get along: a betta takes a guppy's flowing fins for a rival's, and guppies nip in return.
{b} nip long fins; a betta's are the first to go.
{b} are fin nippers: slow fish with long fins like {a} get harried.
Grown angelfish eat fish the size of {b}.
Angelfish and bettas both defend their space, and the one with longer fins loses.
{a} eat whatever fits in their mouth; most community fish do.
{b} hunt shrimp, shrimplets above all; a thickly planted tank saves some.
Goldfish like it cool (18–22 °C) and tropical fish warm; one of them is always out of its range.
Mbuna cichlids are territorial and want hard, alkaline water; soft-water community fish get bullied and stressed.
Loaches eat snails, {b} included; good if that's the plan, not if they're pets.
Tiger barbs nip the long feelers of gouramis.
Two kinds of clownfish in one tank fight over the anemone and the territory; one pair is the rule.

groups.text: Two bettas in one tank fight, male or female alike, unless it's a large, planted sorority of several females watched closely.
Paradise fish males fight like bettas; keep one male.
